How does 'The Middleness of the Middle Way' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"As the defilements gradually become weaker, the matters of the Dhamma—concentration, mindfulness, discernment, persistence—become stronger and stronger."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. In 'The Middleness of the Middle Way', what insight is conveyed by the reflection on: 'He’s first gain Awakening, making...'?

The text reflects: *"He’s the first to gain Awakening, making his way all by himself past the enemy army of defilement, craving, and mental effluents, to proclaim the Dhamma to the world so that we can study it and put it into practice, which is our great good fortune."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.
